strengths: Addresses an important and timely open question in atomistic machine learning: whether machine learning Hamiltonians (MLHs) can achieve the energy and force accuracy of dedicated interatomic potentials (MLIPs) under direct functional evaluation, resolving recent skepticism in the literature.

Principled and effective architectural design: QHFlow2 combines an efficient SO(2)-equivariant message-passing backbone with a two-stage pairwise refinement (SO(2) initialization + SO(3) tensor-product refinement) and flow matching, achieving a 40–50% error reduction over prior state-of-the-art Hamiltonian predictors with fewer parameters and faster inference.

Outstanding downstream performance across multiple benchmarks: on MD17/rMD17, QHFlow2 is the first Hamiltonian model to reach NequIP-level force accuracy while yielding up to 20x lower energy MAE; on QH9, it outperforms strong MLIPs such as MACE and EquiformerV2 in energy metrics.

Exceptional theoretical and physical depth in error analysis: the authors provide a rigorous first-order perturbation explanation showing why energy errors scale quadratically with density error (O(||δH||^2)) while force errors scale linearly (O(||δH||)), supported by empirical log-log scaling fits, MO-basis error decompositions (occupied vs. virtual space), and local PES / Hessian evaluations.
weaknesses: Downstream inference latency: Evaluating energies and analytic forces requires solving the generalized eigenvalue problem and performing a Fock build via PySCF/GPU4PySCF. While this replaces a full SCF iteration, it remains approximately an order of magnitude slower than direct MLIP forward passes (e.g., ~1.5s vs. ~0.1s per structure on MD17).

Non-conservative force nuances: Analytic forces evaluated from a single-shot predicted Hamiltonian stem from a non-self-consistent density matrix and are strictly speaking non-conservative. Although the authors analyze this via finite-difference comparisons in Table 23, conservative dynamics still require full SCF convergence.

Cross-benchmark comparisons on QH9: For the QH9 results against MLIPs (Figure 3 and Table 16), MLIP values are taken from published QM9 benchmarks rather than retrained on the exact identical QH9 split, which introduces minor inconsistencies in training setup.

Scope limited to closed-shell systems with fixed basis sets: The framework currently targets restricted closed-shell systems under a fixed exchange-correlation functional and basis set, requiring retraining if the underlying quantum chemistry setup changes.

strengths: Significance and benchmark impact: The paper bridges an important gap between machine learning Hamiltonians (MLHs) and machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). By re-evaluating MLHs on direct energy and force prediction, it demonstrates for the first time that MLH models can reach MLIP-level force accuracy while substantially improving energy accuracy (up to 20x lower energy MAE than NequIP on MD17/rMD17).

Novel and principled architecture: QHFlow2 smartly combines an efficient SO(2)-equivariant message-passing backbone (adapted from eSEN) with a two-stage pair update module (SO(2) initialization followed by SO(3) tensor-product coupling) and flow matching. This design addresses previous cutoff sensitivity issues in off-diagonal Hamiltonian block prediction while improving parameter efficiency and inference throughput.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation and scaling: The experimental validation is remarkably thorough, covering multiple standard and diverse datasets (MD17, rMD17, QH9, nablaDFT/∇2DFT, and zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluation on PubChem up to 98 atoms). The paper also systematically demonstrates model scaling up to ~1B parameters and data scaling.

Deep theoretical and physical analysis: The manuscript provides extensive diagnostic investigations, including a perturbative analysis explaining why energy errors scale quadratically with density errors while force errors scale linearly, an MO-basis block-wise error decomposition, finite-difference force consistency checks, and local PES curvature / Hessian evaluations.
weaknesses: Downstream computational throughput bottleneck: As acknowledged in the limitations and Table 18, evaluating energies and forces directly from the predicted Hamiltonian requires solving a generalized eigenvalue problem and performing a single Fock build (Coulomb J and XC evaluation in PySCF). This incurs ~1.5s per evaluation compared to ~0.1s for standard MLIPs, making direct MD rollouts significantly slower than MLIP baselines despite faster NN inference.

Non-conservative nature of one-shot forces: Because the predicted Hamiltonian yields a density that is not strictly self-consistent with respect to the Kohn-Sham equations, the resulting analytic gradients are not strictly conservative without running additional SCF iterations.

Minor editorial oversights: There are several typographical and formatting slips, such as an incomplete sentence at the bottom of Page 1 ('Under the extended benchmark, we show that sufficiently' transitioning abruptly to Page 2), missing punctuation on Page 5 ('...and we will release the benchmark Full dataset construction...'), and footnote numbering formatting ('MDsim framework0' on Page 25).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question in atomistic machine learning: whether machine learning Hamiltonians (MLHs) can match or surpass machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) in direct energy and force prediction accuracy.

QHFlow2 introduces a well-motivated architecture combining an SO(2)-equivariant message-passing backbone (adapted from eSEN) with an explicit two-stage pairwise feature update (SO(2) initialization followed by SO(3) tensor-product refinement), demonstrating improved parameter efficiency and robustness across interaction cutoffs.

Comprehensive empirical validation across MD17, rMD17, QH9, and ∇2DFT benchmarks. On MD17/rMD17, QHFlow2 is the first MLH to reach NequIP-level force accuracy while delivering up to 20× lower energy MAE; on QH9, it significantly outperforms MACE and EquiformerV2 on energy prediction.

Provides deep physical and theoretical insights, including a first-order perturbation theory derivation explaining why energy errors scale quadratically (O(||δH||²)) while force errors scale linearly (O(||δH||)) with respect to density/Hamiltonian errors, which is empirically validated via log-log regression.

Thorough MO-basis block decomposition and PES analysis (geometry optimization, finite-difference Hessians, and vibrational frequencies) revealing why elementwise Hamiltonian MAE does not strictly correlate with energy accuracy and showing that QHFlow2 faithfully captures local PES curvature.
weaknesses: Inference latency: While QHFlow2 is faster than prior MLH models, direct evaluation of energy and forces requires solving the generalized eigenvalue problem and performing a single Fock matrix build (evaluating Coulomb and XC integrals via PySCF/GPU4PySCF). As shown in Table 18, total per-sample evaluation time (~1.5 s) is approximately an order of magnitude slower than direct MLIP forward passes (~0.09–0.17 s), limiting high-throughput molecular dynamics.

Generalization to larger systems: Zero-shot transfer experiments on PubChem molecules (Table 21) show severe degradation in energy MAE and SCF cycle ratio for molecules with 80–98 atoms due to orbital ill-conditioning near the frontier band edge, indicating limitations when scaling beyond small organic molecules.

Non-conservative force fields: Because forces are computed analytically from a one-shot, non-self-consistent density matrix, they are not guaranteed to be strictly conservative gradients of the one-shot energy functional across the entire potential energy surface.

Setup specificity: Models are inherently tied to fixed DFT configurations (specific XC functional and GTO basis set) and require computing the exact basis overlap matrix S for each molecular geometry.
